comment.text: Any idea why it's called hydration??

ext.text_original: Any idea why it's called hydration??

preview_replies.textDisplay:
This is what Claude tells me and I think it makes a lot of sense. 🫣

The term comes from a metaphor about adding "water" to something "dry" to bring it back to life. When a server renders HTML, it produces static, non-interactive markup — a "dehydrated" version of your app. It has the right structure and content, but none of the JavaScript event listeners, state, or interactivity are attached. It's like freeze-dried food: the shape is there, but the life is missing.

Hydration is the process of "adding water back" — the client-side JavaScript walks through that existing server-rendered DOM, attaches event handlers, initializes component state, and makes everything interactive again. You're rehydrating the dry HTML into a fully living application.

comment.text: why we can't use page.waitForSelector("locator", { state : 'visible',  timeout : 5000, poll : 500}) ?

ext.text_original: why we can't use page.waitForSelector("locator", { state : 'visible',  timeout : 5000, poll : 500}) ?

preview_replies.textDisplay:
Great question. :) 

Because waiting for an element to become visible is not the problem with these poor hydration patterns. The problem is that the UI looks ready but isn't, and PWT clicks something that doesn't do anything because JS isn't loaded yet.

The described approach recommends retrying actions and assertions with `toPass` so that `click` and `toBeVsisble` run in a loop and are retried for an element. It's pretty much trying a set of instructions multiple times.

I hope this makes sense. :)

preview_replies.textDisplay:
I 100% agree. 

If an application has a poor user experience under slow network conditions, this is a problem and should be fixed.

In the real world, though, and especially when testing and development are different teams, improving the Frontend is rarely prioritized. 

It's the typical "works on my machine" and often, people state the "Playwright is too fast" argument, completely ignoring that the issue often is poor hydration patterns or a broken app under slow network conditions.

`toPass` and other ways to come around test flakiness are workarounds for symptoms and not addressing the root course. But sometimes it is how it is. :) 

So you're 100% right.

comment.text:
Another great video; thank you.

I’d possibly disagree with the “right fix” advice on Playwright’s docs to disable interactive controls until after hydration though, as that could cause confusion and frustration to screen reader users. They might attempt to interact with an element initially announced as being disabled/dimmed, and when that control was subsequently enabled via hydration then you’d have to manage how to update that state to the screen reader user.

preview_replies.textDisplay: Love this comment! You make a great point. I followed the PWT docs for the sake of the storyline of the video. But I think you're correct. Disabled controls aren't focusable and won't trigger validations — and generally in the UX/a11y community it's advised to not disable controls for these reasons. But yeah, the topic of poor hydration + disabled controls is probably for another day and/or video. Thanks! 💙

preview_replies.textDisplay: @yt-channel-117 you. It was more of an end-user issue I was highlighting (not necessarily Playwright operation); that it’s not great to set out a page as having x elements non-operable and to then amend that, as it’s something that then possibly has to be managed so the screen reader user is aware they can use those elements. It might be edge-case; that the page will hydrate and elements are enabled before a screen reader user attempts to use those elements, but it might be more of-a-thing in things like modals (where you often have a button default-focused).
